title: Lecanemab for early-stage Alzheimer's disease
intro: Lecanemab is an antibody medicine given by infusion that targets amyloid, a protein that builds up in the brain in Alzheimer's disease. It is intended for people in the early stages and may modestly slow the decline in memory and thinking. It does not cure the disease and carries notable risks, so careful assessment is required.

sections.heading: How it works
paragraphs: In Alzheimer's disease, clumps of amyloid protein form plaques between nerve cells. Lecanemab attaches to amyloid and helps the immune system clear it from the brain. Researchers think reducing amyloid may slow disease progression, although exactly how much this translates into everyday benefit is debated.

sections.heading: Who may be considered
paragraphs: The medicine is intended for people with mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to Alzheimer's disease in whom amyloid has been confirmed by a brain scan or spinal fluid test. People with certain risk factors, such as bleeding in the brain, use of blood thinners or genetic features that raise the chance of side effects, may not be suitable. Availability and approval differ between countries.

sections.heading: What studies found
paragraphs: In a large trial lasting eighteen months, people receiving lecanemab declined somewhat more slowly on a rating scale than people receiving placebo. The difference was small, and experts disagree about whether it is noticeable in daily life. Longer-term benefits are still being studied.

sections.heading: Risks and monitoring
paragraphs: Treatment is given as an infusion every two weeks, and brain scans are needed before and during treatment. A known side effect is swelling or small bleeds in the brain, called amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Most are without symptoms, but some cause headache, confusion or dizziness, and rarely they can be serious. People who carry two copies of a gene variant called APOE4 are at higher risk. Infusion reactions such as fever or chills may also occur.

sections.heading: Making a decision
paragraphs: The decision involves weighing a modest possible slowing of decline against regular infusions, scans, risks and burden on the family. Talk with a specialist about your goals. Support, medicines for symptoms, activity, social contact and care planning remain important with or without this treatment.

examples.title: Preparing for a specialist visit
examples.text: Imagine you have been diagnosed with early Alzheimer's. You could write down questions about whether you qualify, what the benefits are in everyday life and what the monitoring involves, and bring a relative along.

examples.title: Weighing the burden
examples.text: Suppose you live far from the hospital. You might discuss how often travel would be needed for infusions and scans and whether this fits with your daily life.
